system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2185-11-03 20:14:00 to 2185-11-04 19:03:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was readmitted less than 24 hours after discharge due to sudden, severe right hip pain. He has a complex history including end-stage renal disease, recent MRSA line infection, non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, and avascular necrosis of the right femoral head. Imaging confirmed advanced avascular necrosis with joint collapse and effusion, raising concern for possible infection. A fluoroscopic-guided hip aspiration was performed, yielding 0.5 mL of fluid. Gram stain showed no organisms, and cultures remained negative, ruling out septic arthritis. Pain was controlled with oxycodone, and vancomycin was discontinued after completion of therapy for prior MRSA infection. The patient was discharged home with services, advised to follow up with orthopedics for evaluation of hip replacement, and given updated medication instructions.
problems: Avascular necrosis of the right femoral head
Pain in joint, pelvic region and thigh

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ man with end-stage renal disease with left subclavian
hemodialysis catheter that was pulled back.  Request exchange of hemodialysis
catheter.  Patient also with extremely difficult access.

OPERATORS:  ___.

ANESTHESIA:  After the midline catheter was placed as described below sedation
was provided by anesthesia.  Please refer to their report for additional
detail.

Upon arrival the anesthesia team attempted to gain access via the right and
left neck; however, given patient discomfort it was decided to place a midline
catheter in the left arm.

PROCEDURE:

1.  Left midline catheter placement.

2.  Tunneled hemodialysis catheter exchange via left subclavian vein.

FINDINGS:

After the risks and benefits of the procedure were explained to the patient,
written informed consent was obtained.  A preprocedure timeout was performed.

MIDLINE CATHETER PLACEMENT:

Under ultrasound and fluoroscopic guidance the left brachial vein was
punctured with a 21-gauge micropuncture needle through which a 0.018 wire was
advanced into the left subclavian vein.  The needle was exchanged for a
micropuncture sheath.  Copy ultrasound images were saved.

A single-lumen 4 ___ PICC was cut to 15 cm and advanced over a nitinol wire
into the left axillary region.  The wire was removed and the catheter was
aspirated and flushed without issue.

The catheter was secured to the skin with a Statlock.  This catheter was used
as access for anesthesia for the tunneled hemodialysis catheter exchange.

TUNNELED HEMODIALYSIS CATHETER EXCHANGE:

The indwelling left subclavian tunneled hemodialysis catheter tip was noted to
be in the cavoatrial junction; however, the cuff was visualized outside of the
tunnel exit site.  Two Amplatz wires were advanced through the catheter after
each lumen was completely aspirated of heparin.  The wires were placed into
the right atrium and the catheter was removed over the two Amplatz wires.  A
new 31 cm tip-to-cuff hemodialysis catheter was advanced over the wires with
tip terminating in the right atrium without issue.  The wires were removed and
the catheter was aspirated and flushed easily.  The catheter was secured to
the skin with 0 silk suture.

There were no immediate complications.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Successful exchange of left subclavian tunneled hemodialysis catheter with
tip terminating in the right atrium.  The line is ready to use.

2.  Successful placement of left midline catheter into the left basilic vein. 
This catheter was placed due to inability to gain access for anesthesia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand your dialysis line came loose today. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it pulled out a bit at daycare. I was moving around and suddenly felt it shift. They couldn’t get any IV access, so they sent me here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had trouble with access before. We’ll need to fix the line. Interventional radiology will replace it under light sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? Last time I had a line infection with MRSA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of your history. The team will use sterile technique, and we’ll monitor closely. No signs of infection now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure is done. They replaced your left subclavian dialysis line successfully. A midline was placed to help with sedation access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can I eat now? I’ve been NPO since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can start eating. We’ll get you something soon. You also had dialysis earlier and they removed about 3 liters of fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been feeling swollen in my legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed some pitting edema. Your dry weight is 84.7 kg, and you were over that. Dialysis helped bring your blood pressure down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying, but sometimes I forget to check my weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s important to weigh yourself daily. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We checked your labs last night. Your potassium was a bit high at 5.7, but dialysis corrected that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I change my diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep avoiding high-potassium foods like bananas and oranges. Your other labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nursing also noted pressure ulcers on your left gluteal area. They’re not infected, but you’ll need wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I sit on my scooter a lot. Should I change how I sit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, reposition every 30 minutes. Avoid putting all your weight on the left side. A home health nurse will help with wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re clearing you to go home. Your line is working, and you’re stable after dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are my medications the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no changes. Keep taking oxycodone for hip pain, gabapentin, Keppra, and all your other meds as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume your regular schedule. The center will contact you. Make sure you’re home on time for visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Sometimes I lose track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re referring you to a new service to help with that. It’s important for your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your midline was removed earlier. The dialysis line is secure and ready for use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up with your doctors. We’ll see you if anything changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted due to partial dislodgement of his left subclavian tunneled hemodialysis catheter, occurring during agitation at daycare. Given his history of difficult vascular access and prior MRSA line infections, interventional radiology successfully replaced the dialysis line under MAC anesthesia, using a left midline catheter for procedural access. The new line was placed without complications and confirmed functional. He underwent dialysis with removal of 3 liters of fluid, improving volume overload. Pressure ulcers were noted at the left gluteal fold, and the patient was counseled on repositioning and wound care. All home medications were continued without change. He was discharged home with services, advised to resume regular dialysis, monitor daily weight, and follow up with outpatient support for visit compliance.
